Before this PR:

After this PR:

- Broadcasts job lifecycle events (`job.created`, `job.started`, `job.progress`, `job.completed`) from API/gRPC paths.

prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:
- Frontend pages relied on manual refresh/polling patterns, so job and agent state updates were delayed.
- Backup lifecycle transitions and progress visibility were not reflected live in the UI.
- Agent connectivity and heartbeat changes were not propagated immediately to operators.

After this PR:
- Adds server-side WebSocket infrastructure and frontend WebSocket client integration for real-time push updates.
- Broadcasts job lifecycle events (`job.created`, `job.started`, `job.progress`, `job.completed`) from API/gRPC paths.
- Broadcasts agent lifecycle events (`agent.connected`, `agent.disconnected`, `agent.heartbeat`, `agent.registered`) from gRPC paths.
- Updates dashboard, job detail, and agent detail stores/views to react to these events without page reload.

Fixes #2, fixes #10

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

Polling was causing stale UX and avoidable load. A WebSocket push model provides low-latency updates and keeps multiple browser tabs consistent during active backups and agent state transitions.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- Uses an in-memory broadcast hub without persistence/replay in v1.
- Uses a broadcast-to-all-clients model (no per-topic filtering/subscriptions yet).
- WS endpoint auth posture matches current REST posture and can be tightened later.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Polling-only updates (simpler, but higher latency and less efficient).
- Server-Sent Events (good one-way streaming, but less flexible for future bidirectional/subscription needs).

Links to places where the discussion took place:
- https://github.com/tryy3/backup-orchestrator/issues/2
- https://github.com/tryy3/backup-orchestrator/issues/10
- docs/realtime-updates.md

### Breaking changes

None expected. The change is additive; existing REST/gRPC flows remain in place.

If this PR introduces breaking changes, please describe the changes and the impact on users.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- New WebSocket server endpoint: `GET /api/ws`
- New server event hub added under `server/internal/events/`
- Frontend reconnect handling is included; verify reconnect and multi-tab behavior during review.
- Job lifecycle now explicitly includes `planned -> running -> success|partial|failed`.

prs.title: ci: replace QEMU cross-compilation with native-arch matrix builds via docker/github-builder
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR: The `Build and Push` GitHub Actions workflow built multi-platform Docker images (`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`) on a single `ubuntu-latest` (amd64) runner using QEMU emulation via `docker/setup-qemu-action`. This made arm64 builds significantly slower due to cross-compilation through emulation.

After this PR: The workflow uses Docker's official `docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1` reusable workflow. It automatically distributes the build across native runner architectures (amd64 and arm64) in parallel, builds each platform natively, then assembles and pushes a single multi-arch manifest. QEMU, manual Buildx setup, and `docker/build-push-action` steps are removed entirely.

Fixes #19
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR: The `Build and Push` GitHub Actions workflow built multi-platform Docker images (`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`) on a single `ubuntu-latest` (amd64) runner using QEMU emulation via `docker/setup-qemu-action`. This made arm64 builds significantly slower due to cross-compilation through emulation.

After this PR: The workflow uses Docker's official `docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1` reusable workflow. It automatically distributes the build across native runner architectures (amd64 and arm64) in parallel, builds each platform natively, then assembles and pushes a single multi-arch manifest. QEMU, manual Buildx setup, and `docker/build-push-action` steps are removed entirely.

Fixes #19

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:
- Delegated build orchestration entirely to Docker's official reusable workflow instead of maintaining the step configuration manually. This reduces per-repo config surface area at the cost of depending on an external reusable workflow (`docker/github-builder`).
- Used `docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1` (the official Docker-maintained solution) rather than writing a manual matrix + manifest-merge job pattern. The reusable workflow handles Buildx setup, cache wiring, SLSA provenance signing, and manifest creation automatically.

The following alternatives were considered:
- **Manual matrix + digest merge**: Define a `strategy.matrix` per platform, build each with `push-by-digest=true`, upload digests as artifacts, and merge via `docker buildx imagetools create`. Functionally equivalent but significantly more verbose to maintain.
- **Keep QEMU + Buildx with tuning**: Does not fundamentally fix the slowness — emulated builds remain slow regardless of tuning.

Links to places where the discussion took place: #19

### Breaking changes

None. Image names, tag patterns, and registry remain unchanged. The multi-arch manifest continues to cover `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`.

### Special notes for your reviewer

The `workflow_dispatch` trigger is intentionally retained for easy manual testing. Signed SLSA provenance attestations are generated automatically by the reusable workflow (`sign: auto` default).

prs.title: feat(agent): add redacted structured logging for external commands
prs.releaseNote: Improve agent-side external command observability by logging structured restic execution context (command, args, env) with sensitive value redaction, and add logging of internally-supplied hook context values.
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR:
- Restic command execution logs did not include enough runtime context to debug failures quickly.
- Sensitive values (for example command/env values) had no centralized redaction utility for command logging.
- Hook execution logged lifecycle events, but not the internal context values injected by the agent into templates.

After this PR:
- Adds structured "executing command" logs for every restic invocation, including command, args, and env context.
- Adds a new internal redaction package to mask sensitive env/arg values in logs (for example `RESTIC_PASSWORD=*****`).
- Threads logger context through `ResticExecutor` methods and updates all call sites.
- Logs internally-provided hook template context (and timeout) without logging user-authored hook commands.
- Adds unit tests for redaction behavior.

Fixes #3
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:
- Restic command execution logs did not include enough runtime context to debug failures quickly.
- Sensitive values (for example command/env values) had no centralized redaction utility for command logging.
- Hook execution logged lifecycle events, but not the internal context values injected by the agent into templates.

After this PR:
- Adds structured "executing command" logs for every restic invocation, including command, args, and env context.
- Adds a new internal redaction package to mask sensitive env/arg values in logs (for example `RESTIC_PASSWORD=*****`).
- Threads logger context through `ResticExecutor` methods and updates all call sites.
- Logs internally-provided hook template context (and timeout) without logging user-authored hook commands.
- Adds unit tests for redaction behavior.

Fixes #3

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

When backups fail, operators need actionable execution context to separate product bugs from configuration/runtime issues. This change improves observability of internally-generated external commands while minimizing leakage risk by redacting sensitive values.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- Uses simple pattern-based redaction (`password`, `secret`, `token`, `credential`) for now; this is intentionally conservative and easy to evolve.
- Logs only command-specific extra env values rather than full inherited process environment.
- For hooks, logs only internal context values and timeout, not user-authored script content.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Logging full command/environment without redaction (rejected due to secret exposure risk).
- Redacting all argument values broadly (rejected because it would remove useful debugging context).
- Logging expanded hook command text (rejected per requirement to avoid logging user input).

Links to places where the discussion took place: None

### Breaking changes

If this PR introduces breaking changes, please describe the changes and the impact on users.

None.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- The logging signature change adds `*slog.Logger` parameters across `ResticExecutor` methods; reviewers should verify all call sites were updated.
- Redaction behavior is covered by unit tests under `agent/internal/redact`.

### Checklist

A new reusable `RunHeatmap` component (inspired by GitHub's contribution graph) replaces the histogram, showing the last 30 runs per agent on the fleet overview and per plan on the agent detail page. Each cell is color-coded (green=success, amber=partial, red=failed), hoverable (shows status, date, duration), and clickable (navigates to the job detail page).

![Fleet Overview with heatmaps](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b5ac0804-aaab-41ac-a022-aaed73c87c92)

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

Red is a strong signal that something is currently broken. Using it for historical job failures creates false urgency and masks whether the agent itself is reachable. The fix separates the two concerns at the color/indicator level and replaces the histogram with a more intuitive heatmap visualization focused on runs rather than days.

**New component: `RunHeatmap.vue`**
- Reusable heatmap component at `frontend/src/components/common/RunHeatmap.vue`
- Displays the last N completed runs as colored cells (green=success, amber=partial, red=failed)
- Hover tooltip shows status, plan name, date, and duration
- Click navigates to the job detail page via `router.push(/jobs/:id)`
- `@click.stop.prevent` prevents parent link navigation when clicking a cell inside a `<router-link>`
- Empty slots render as dimmed cells to maintain consistent width

**DashboardView.vue**
- New `connectivityDotClass(agent)` — green when online, slate when offline. Replaces `statusDotClass` which mixed in job history.
- Card border for `'failing'` changed from `border-red-500` → `border-orange-500`
- Filter renamed "Failing" → "Job Issues" with orange dot
- Replaced 30-day sparkline histogram with `RunHeatmap` showing last 30 runs per agent (all plans combined)
- Reliability text and global success rate: red → orange

**AgentDetailView.vue**
- `failedPlanIds` now derived from `latestJobByPlan` (latest job per plan only) instead of scanning all historical jobs
- Failing plan alert: red → amber, message updated to "with a failed latest run"
- Replaced stats/sparkline section with combined "Recent Runs" heatmap for all agent jobs
- Replaced plan table with card layout — each plan card includes its own per-plan `RunHeatmap`

The following tradeoffs were made:

- `agentHealthStatus()` still factors job history for filtering/counting — only the visual treatment changed. This keeps the filter categories useful without implying the agent itself is down.
- Heatmap shows last 30 runs (hardcoded) — may be made configurable in the future.
- Focus shifted from "past few days" to "past few runs" for more meaningful per-run granularity.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Keeping the histogram but adding hover/click — rejected because the histogram's variable-height bars were visually confusing and didn't map well to individual runs.
- Removing job history from the fleet overview entirely — rejected because the heatmap and reliability % are valuable context.
- Adding a separate "agent health" API endpoint — unnecessary since heartbeat timestamps already provide connectivity status client-side.

None. Pure UI/presentation change with no API or data model modifications.

prs.title: Refactor Restic repository initialization and error handling
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR: The agent had no unit tests, the scheduler lacked context-based
cancellation, MultiHandler stopped at the first handler error, the Reporter had
no retry cap, and restic repository initialization used fragile stderr-string
matching to decide whether to call `init`.

After this PR:
- `executor/restic.go`: Simplified `EnsureRepo` — always attempts `init` on
  snapshot-check failure; treats "already initialized" / "already exists" as
  success, removing the fragile pre-check on stderr strings.
- `grpcclient`: Build-time version variables (`AgentVersion`, `ResticVersion`,
  `RcloneVersion`) injected into registration requests.
- `grpcclient/stream.go`: Minor robustness improvements.
- `logging/buffer.go`: `BufferHandler` now supports attribute grouping with
  prefixed keys.
- `logging/multi.go`: `MultiHandler` collects errors from all handlers instead
  of short-circuiting on the first failure.
- `reporter/reporter.go`: Added a max-flush-attempts constant to drop reports
  that exceed the retry limit.
- `scheduler/scheduler.go`: Scheduler now accepts and propagates a cancellable
  `context.Context` for running jobs.
- Unit tests added for: `database`, `executor/hooks`, `identity`, `logging/buffer`,
  `reporter`, `scheduler`.
- Docs: `agent-further-considerations.md` and `agent-internal-review.md` added
  as internal design notes.

Fixes #

### What this PR does

Before this PR: The agent had no unit tests, the scheduler lacked context-based
cancellation, MultiHandler stopped at the first handler error, the Reporter had
no retry cap, and restic repository initialization used fragile stderr-string
matching to decide whether to call `init`.

After this PR:
- `executor/restic.go`: Simplified `EnsureRepo` — always attempts `init` on
  snapshot-check failure; treats "already initialized" / "already exists" as
  success, removing the fragile pre-check on stderr strings.
- `grpcclient`: Build-time version variables (`AgentVersion`, `ResticVersion`,
  `RcloneVersion`) injected into registration requests.
- `grpcclient/stream.go`: Minor robustness improvements.
- `logging/buffer.go`: `BufferHandler` now supports attribute grouping with
  prefixed keys.
- `logging/multi.go`: `MultiHandler` collects errors from all handlers instead
  of short-circuiting on the first failure.
- `reporter/reporter.go`: Added a max-flush-attempts constant to drop reports
  that exceed the retry limit.
- `scheduler/scheduler.go`: Scheduler now accepts and propagates a cancellable
  `context.Context` for running jobs.
- Unit tests added for: `database`, `executor/hooks`, `identity`, `logging/buffer`,
  `reporter`, `scheduler`.
- Docs: `agent-further-considerations.md` and `agent-internal-review.md` added
  as internal design notes.

Fixes #

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The agent had grown without tests or defensive error handling, making future
changes risky. This refactor adds coverage and tightens the most error-prone
paths before new features are built on top.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- `EnsureRepo` now always calls `init` on failure rather than pre-checking stderr
  content. This is simpler and more robust — restic's own output determines
  success, not our string matching.
- Reporter retry cap uses a simple counter rather than an exponential backoff
  queue to keep the implementation minimal.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Keeping stderr-based repo detection: rejected because the exact error strings
  differ across restic versions.

None.

prs.title: refactor(server): context propagation, HTTP/gRPC hardening, resource cleanup, and tests
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR:
- Database methods had no context propagation — long-running queries could not be cancelled
- HTTP server had no read/write/idle timeouts — connections could hang indefinitely
- The event hub and agent manager had no `Close()` method — goroutines could leak on shutdown
- The gRPC server used single interceptors with no panic recovery — a panic in any handler would crash the server
- `Register` RPC returned a plain `fmt.Errorf` instead of a gRPC status error — clients received `codes.Unknown`
- The stream auth interceptor did not inject the authenticated agent ID into the stream context
- `connect.go` queried the DB on every heartbeat message to check agent status
- `configpush/resolver.go` loaded repositories one at a time in a loop (N+1 queries)
- Shutdown in `main.go` stopped HTTP/gRPC but did not tear down the agent manager or event hub
- No tests existed for any of the above subsystems

After this PR:
- All 43 database methods accept `context.Context` and use `ExecContext`/`QueryContext`/`QueryRowContext`/`BeginTx`
- HTTP server has `ReadTimeout=30s`, `WriteTimeout=60s`, `IdleTimeout=120s`
- `events.Hub` and `agentmgr.Manager` both have idempotent `Close()` methods using `sync.Once`
- gRPC server uses `ChainUnaryInterceptor`/`ChainStreamInterceptor` with a panic recovery interceptor that returns `codes.Internal` and logs the stack trace
- `Register` RPC returns `status.Errorf(codes.Internal, ...)` on DB error
- Stream auth injects agent ID into stream context via a `wrappedServerStream`
- Agent status is cached in `connect.go` with a 60-second refresh interval
- Repository loading in `configpush` uses a single `WHERE id IN (...)` batch query (`GetRepositoriesByIDs`)
- `main.go` shutdown calls `mgr.Close()` then `hub.Close()` after the HTTP/gRPC servers stop
- 42 tests added across `database`, `events`, and `agentmgr` packages with `-race` detection passing

Fixes #
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:
- Database methods had no context propagation — long-running queries could not be cancelled
- HTTP server had no read/write/idle timeouts — connections could hang indefinitely
- The event hub and agent manager had no `Close()` method — goroutines could leak on shutdown
- The gRPC server used single interceptors with no panic recovery — a panic in any handler would crash the server
- `Register` RPC returned a plain `fmt.Errorf` instead of a gRPC status error — clients received `codes.Unknown`
- The stream auth interceptor did not inject the authenticated agent ID into the stream context
- `connect.go` queried the DB on every heartbeat message to check agent status
- `configpush/resolver.go` loaded repositories one at a time in a loop (N+1 queries)
- Shutdown in `main.go` stopped HTTP/gRPC but did not tear down the agent manager or event hub
- No tests existed for any of the above subsystems

After this PR:
- All 43 database methods accept `context.Context` and use `ExecContext`/`QueryContext`/`QueryRowContext`/`BeginTx`
- HTTP server has `ReadTimeout=30s`, `WriteTimeout=60s`, `IdleTimeout=120s`
- `events.Hub` and `agentmgr.Manager` both have idempotent `Close()` methods using `sync.Once`
- gRPC server uses `ChainUnaryInterceptor`/`ChainStreamInterceptor` with a panic recovery interceptor that returns `codes.Internal` and logs the stack trace
- `Register` RPC returns `status.Errorf(codes.Internal, ...)` on DB error
- Stream auth injects agent ID into stream context via a `wrappedServerStream`
- Agent status is cached in `connect.go` with a 60-second refresh interval
- Repository loading in `configpush` uses a single `WHERE id IN (...)` batch query (`GetRepositoriesByIDs`)
- `main.go` shutdown calls `mgr.Close()` then `hub.Close()` after the HTTP/gRPC servers stop
- 42 tests added across `database`, `events`, and `agentmgr` packages with `-race` detection passing

Fixes #

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

These are hardening and correctness fixes identified in a two-pass code review of the server codebase.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- Context is propagated from `r.Context()` at the HTTP handler boundary; goroutine-based config pushes use `context.Background()` since they outlive the request.
- Agent status caching (60s TTL) trades strict consistency for reduced DB load on high-frequency heartbeat paths.
- `sync.Once` is used for `Close()` to allow safe double-close without panics.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Using a cache library for agent status instead of manual TTL — deferred as overkill for a single field.
- `GetRepositoriesByIDs` uses string concatenation for the `IN` clause with validated UUID inputs; a prepared statement with array binding is not supported by the SQLite driver without reflection tricks.

Links to places where the discussion took place: tracked in `docs/server-internal-fixes.md` and `docs/server-further-consideration.md`

### Breaking changes

None. All changes are internal to the server package. The REST and gRPC API contracts are unchanged.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- `docs/server-internal-fixes.md` and `docs/server-further-consideration.md` document the full finding list and rationale for each change.
- Three items from the review were deliberately deferred to separate issues: config push race (#47), settings free-form key/value (#48), and CORS (#45).

prs.title: feat: migrate to justfile, add CI pipeline, lefthook pre-commit hooks, golangci-lint
prs.breakingChanges: `make <target>` no longer works. All targets are available via `just <recipe>` with equivalent or expanded functionality. Run `just` to list all available recipes.
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
**Before this PR:** Makefile with build and Docker targets only. No test/lint/fmt aliases, no pre-commit hooks, no CI quality checks (tests, linting, formatting).

**After this PR:** Full developer tooling stack — just task runner, lefthook pre-commit hooks, golangci-lint config, and a parallel CI pipeline.

---

**`justfile`** (replaces `Makefile`)

Organized recipe groups: `test`, `test-cover`, `fmt`, `vet`, `lint`, `build`, `proto-*`, `docker-*`, `clean` — all available per-module (`-server`, `-agent`) and aggregated. `docker-push` requires confirmation (`[confirm]`). Run `just` to list all recipes.

**`.golangci.yml`**

Enables: `errcheck`, `ineffassign`, `staticcheck`, `unused`, `gocritic`, `gofmt`, `misspell`, `noctx`, `bodyclose`, `gosimple`, `prealloc`. Relaxed ruleset for test files.

**`.lefthook.yml`**

Pre-commit only: `gofmt` check + `go vet` on staged Go files. Deliberately no tests or golangci-lint — keeps hooks under 5s so developers don't bypass with `--no-verify`.

**`.github/workflows/ci.yml`**

Parallel jobs split by when they should run:

| Job | Trigger |
|---|---|
| `test-server`, `test-agent` (`go test -race`) | Every push |
| `test-frontend` (vitest) | Every push |
| `fmt-vet` (gofmt check + go vet) | Every push |
| `build` (frontend + server + agent) | Every push |
| `lint` (golangci-lint) | PRs only |
| `proto-check` (buf lint + breaking change detection) | PRs only |

**`flake.nix`** — adds `just` and `lefthook` to the Nix dev shell.

**`CLAUDE.md`** — replaces the old build commands section with full `just` and `lefthook` documentation.
prs.body:
Developer tooling and CI were minimal: Makefile had build/docker targets only, no test/lint/fmt commands, no pre-commit hooks, and no quality gates in CI beyond Docker image builds.

### What this PR does

**Before this PR:** Makefile with build and Docker targets only. No test/lint/fmt aliases, no pre-commit hooks, no CI quality checks (tests, linting, formatting).

**After this PR:** Full developer tooling stack — just task runner, lefthook pre-commit hooks, golangci-lint config, and a parallel CI pipeline.

---

**`justfile`** (replaces `Makefile`)

Organized recipe groups: `test`, `test-cover`, `fmt`, `vet`, `lint`, `build`, `proto-*`, `docker-*`, `clean` — all available per-module (`-server`, `-agent`) and aggregated. `docker-push` requires confirmation (`[confirm]`). Run `just` to list all recipes.

**`.golangci.yml`**

Enables: `errcheck`, `ineffassign`, `staticcheck`, `unused`, `gocritic`, `gofmt`, `misspell`, `noctx`, `bodyclose`, `gosimple`, `prealloc`. Relaxed ruleset for test files.

**`.lefthook.yml`**

Pre-commit only: `gofmt` check + `go vet` on staged Go files. Deliberately no tests or golangci-lint — keeps hooks under 5s so developers don't bypass with `--no-verify`.

**`.github/workflows/ci.yml`**

Parallel jobs split by when they should run:

| Job | Trigger |
|---|---|
| `test-server`, `test-agent` (`go test -race`) | Every push |
| `test-frontend` (vitest) | Every push |
| `fmt-vet` (gofmt check + go vet) | Every push |
| `build` (frontend + server + agent) | Every push |
| `lint` (golangci-lint) | PRs only |
| `proto-check` (buf lint + breaking change detection) | PRs only |

**`flake.nix`** — adds `just` and `lefthook` to the Nix dev shell.

**`CLAUDE.md`** — replaces the old build commands section with full `just` and `lefthook` documentation.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:
- **just over Make**: Make's file dependency model adds no value here since all builds delegate to `go`, `vite`, and `buf`. Just has cleaner syntax, no tab requirement, built-in `--list`, `.env` loading, and `[confirm]` for dangerous recipes.
- **lefthook over pre-commit**: Single Go binary, fast, YAML config — no Python dependency. Pre-commit hooks are kept minimal (gofmt + vet only) so they remain fast and won't be skipped.
- **golangci-lint on PRs only**: Heavy linting doesn't need to block every branch push; it's the gate that matters before merge.
- **proto-check on PRs only**: Breaking change detection only makes sense against a base branch, which only exists in a PR context.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Keep Makefile — rejected; no file dependency tracking needed, and just provides meaningfully better DX.

Version fields in `Register` and `sendHeartbeat` were hardcoded placeholders. `ResticVersion` in heartbeats was additionally broken — set to the OS/arch string (`linux/amd64`) instead of an actual version.

### What this PR does

Before this PR:
- `AgentVersion`, `ResticVersion`, `RcloneVersion` were static placeholder strings in `grpcclient`
- `sendHeartbeat` sent `fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", runtime.GOOS, runtime.GOARCH)` as `ResticVersion`

After this PR:
- Agent runs `restic version` and `rclone version` at startup to detect real installed versions
- Agent **fails fast** (`os.Exit(1)`) if either binary is missing — no silent degraded operation
- Detected versions flow into both `Register` RPC and every `sendHeartbeat` via existing `grpcclient` package vars
- `AgentVersion` remains injectable at build time via `-ldflags "-X ...grpcclient.AgentVersion=..."`
- Branch rebased onto `main`

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

Accurate version reporting matters for operator visibility and future compatibility checks server-side.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- Version detection sets package-level vars in `grpcclient` rather than threading them through constructors — minimal diff surface, consistent with the existing ldflags pattern for `AgentVersion`
- Parsing is done on the first line of output only (`rclone version` is multi-line; `restic version` is single-line) — sufficient and stable
- `runCommand` captures stderr and includes it in error messages for easier debugging when a binary fails

The following alternatives were considered:
- Accept `--restic-version` / `--rclone-version` config flags as overrides — deferred, can be layered on top later
- Move versions into `Client`/`StreamHandler` constructors — cleaner coupling, but larger refactor out of scope here

prs.body:
The frontend displayed a hard-coded `v0.1.0` string, the server had no version surface, and the agent reported a static placeholder instead of its actual build version.

### What this PR does

**Before this PR:**
- Sidebar shows `v0.1.0` regardless of the actual build.
- `GET /api/version` does not exist; server version is not queryable.
- Agent heartbeats send `"0.1.0-dev"` as a hard-coded literal, so the Agents page "Version" column is meaningless.
- Builds embed no version metadata.

**After this PR:**
- Sidebar shows the value of `VITE_APP_VERSION` (injected at build time), falling back to `"dev"`.
- `GET /api/version` returns `{"version", "commit", "build_date"}` from the server binary.
- Settings page shows an **About** section with frontend version + server version/commit/build date.
- Agent heartbeats report the real binary version; the Agents page "Version" column reflects actual builds.
- `make build-*` injects version metadata into all three components.

### Changes

**New version packages** (`server/internal/version/version.go`, `agent/internal/version/version.go`):
```go
var (
    Version   = "dev"
    Commit    = "unknown"
    BuildDate = "unknown"
)
```
Overridden at link time via `-ldflags "-X .../version.Version=v1.2.3 ..."`.

**Server REST endpoint** (`server/internal/api/version.go`):
- `GET /api/version` → `{"version":"v1.2.3","commit":"abc1234","build_date":"2026-04-09T..."}`

**Agent** (`agent/internal/grpcclient/client.go`):
- `AgentVersion` now reads from `version.Version` instead of a hard-coded string.

**Makefile** — version variables computed once, injected everywhere:
```makefile
VERSION    ?= $(shell git describe --tags --exact-match 2>/dev/null || echo "dev")
COMMIT     ?= $(shell git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo "unknown")
BUILD_DATE ?= $(shell date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
```
- Go: `-ldflags "-X $(SERVER_PKG).Version=$(VERSION) ..."`
- Frontend: `VITE_APP_VERSION=$(VERSION) npm run build`

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:
- `ldflags` injection is the idiomatic Go pattern (Docker, Kubernetes, Hugo all do this). No external files, no runtime detection, zero overhead.
- `VITE_APP_VERSION` is a standard Vite env var approach; no `define` block needed since Vite exposes `VITE_*` vars automatically via `import.meta.env`.
- `ResticVersion` / `RcloneVersion` remain `"unknown"` — these are installed-tool versions requiring runtime detection, which is out of scope here.
- Server version is surfaced in Settings (not a dedicated page) to avoid adding nav items for a small metadata surface.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Runtime `debug.ReadBuildInfo()` — works but returns module path info, not clean semver tags; ldflags is more explicit and universally understood.
- A single root-level version file shared by server and agent — Go modules are separate, so each needs its own package to keep ldflags paths unambiguous.

### Breaking changes

None.

### Special notes for your reviewer

The pre-existing `src/api/__tests__/websocket.test.ts` TS1294 error causes `vue-tsc -b` (used by `npm run build`) to fail — this is unrelated to this PR and was present before these changes. `vite build` and `vue-tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck` both pass cleanly.

prs.title: Implement remote filesystem browser for path selection (#8)
prs.body:
## Summary

Implement a remote filesystem browser that allows users to browse the live filesystem of a connected agent directly from the UI when configuring repository paths and backup plan source paths.

- Users can navigate the agent's directory tree one level at a time
- Requests go through the existing gRPC command/response flow (`BrowseFilesystem` command)
- Agent validates paths and returns only directories via `os.ReadDir`
- Frontend component provides an inline tree dropdown with keyboard navigation support

## Changes

- **Proto**: Added `BrowseFilesystem` message and `browse_filesystem` field to `Command` oneof
- **Agent**: Implemented `BrowseFilesystem` handler with path validation and directory enumeration
- **Server**: Added REST endpoint `GET /api/agents/:id/fs?path=<path>` to forward browse requests
- **Frontend**: Added `FileBrowser` component with tree navigation, client-side caching, and full keyboard support

## Design & Security

See `docs/filesystem-browser-design.md` for full design rationale, UI specs, and security considerations including:
- Absolute path validation and path traversal prevention
- Blocked prefixes (`/proc`, `/sys`, `/dev`, `/run/credentials`)
- Permission error passthrough to the user

## Test Plan

- [ ] Navigate agent filesystem from repository path input
- [ ] Navigate agent filesystem from backup plan source path input
- [ ] Verify path validation (rejection of relative paths, blocked prefixes)
- [ ] Verify permission errors are displayed in the UI
- [ ] Test keyboard navigation (arrow keys, Tab, Enter, Esc)
- [ ] Verify offline agents return 502 Bad Gateway
- [ ] Run `just test` (all tests pass)
- [ ] Run `just build` (builds successfully)

Closes #8

prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:

Selecting a repository type (e.g., `rclone`) required the user to manually type the full restic URI including the backend prefix (`rclone:myremote:bucket`). The type dropdown was decorative — it didn't influence the path.

After this PR:

The type prefix is shown as a read-only input group label adjacent to the path field and auto-prepended on save. Existing repositories with manually-typed prefixes are handled transparently — the prefix is stripped on load and re-applied on save.

![repository form with rclone prefix](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/53144e92-74f6-4908-924e-6497710fa4a6)

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- **Input group label over silent prepend**: A visible `rclone:` / `local:` label makes it obvious what will be stored, avoiding user confusion.
- **Strip-on-load / prepend-on-save**: Backward-compatible with existing repos. Old paths like `rclone:remote:bucket` display as `remote:bucket` with the label, and re-save identically.
- **`formReady` guard on watcher**: The type watcher strips the old prefix when the user changes types mid-edit. A `nextTick`-gated flag prevents the watcher from firing during initial form hydration (where the default `local` → loaded type transition would incorrectly strip path content).
- **Double-prepend guard**: If a user manually types the prefix in the input, `handleSubmit` checks `path.startsWith(prefix)` before prepending.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Silently prepending without visual indicator — rejected because the original issue specifically called out user confusion.
- Server-side prepend — rejected because it would require API contract changes and the frontend already knows the type.

### Breaking changes

None. Existing stored paths are unchanged. The prefix is only applied/stripped in the frontend form layer.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- The `FileBrowser` path (local type + local scope + agent selected) bypasses the prefix label since it has its own UI, but `handleSubmit` still prepends `local:` on save.
- Context-aware placeholders update per type (e.g., `remote:bucket/path` for rclone, `user@host:/path` for sftp).

prs.title: Replace text/template with strings.Replacer for hook command expansion
prs.breakingChanges: Hook commands containing unrecognised `{{.X}}` placeholders no longer return an expansion error; they now execute with the placeholder left as a literal string. This is unlikely to affect any real usage and is strictly safer.
prs.body:
`text/template` was used for `{{.FieldName}}` substitution in hook commands — a full template engine where only literal string replacement is needed. `text/template` can invoke any method on the context value; if `HookContext` ever gains methods, those become callable from server-authored hook strings running via `sh -c`.

### Changes

- **`hooks.go`**: Replace `expandTemplate` implementation with `strings.Replacer` over the fixed `HookContext` field set. Simplify signature from `(string, error)` → `string` (replacer is infallible). Remove `text/template` and `fmt` imports. Drop dead error-check branch in `RunHook`.
- **`hooks_test.go`**: Update call sites to new signature. Replace error-expectation tests (`InvalidTemplate`, `MissingField`) with pass-through behaviour tests — unknown placeholders are now left unchanged rather than returning an error.
- **`docs/agent-further-considerations.md`**: Mark §1 Hook Template Engine Safety as resolved.

**Before:**
```go
func expandTemplate(cmdStr string, hctx *HookContext) (string, error) {
    tmpl, err := template.New("hook").Parse(cmdStr)
    // ...execute into buffer...
}
```

**After:**
```go
func expandTemplate(cmdStr string, hctx *HookContext) string {
    r := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{{.PlanName}}", hctx.PlanName,
        "{{.Hostname}}", hctx.Hostname,
        // ... all HookContext fields ...
    )
    return r.Replace(cmdStr)
}
```

The allowed variable set is now explicit and auditable at a glance. Method-call risk is eliminated by construction.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

No conditional, loop, pipeline, or custom function template logic is used — `text/template` was providing zero value beyond what `strings.Replacer` covers.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- Unknown placeholders now pass through unchanged instead of returning an error. This is the correct behaviour for a literal replacer and avoids failing hooks on typos in non-variable `{{` sequences that happen to appear in shell commands.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Keep `text/template` with a custom `FuncMap` allowlist — more complexity for no benefit given no advanced template logic is needed.
- Document a "no methods on HookContext" constraint — relies on future contributors knowing and respecting an invisible invariant.

### Breaking changes

Hook commands containing unrecognised `{{.X}}` placeholders no longer return an expansion error; they now execute with the placeholder left as a literal string. This is unlikely to affect any real usage and is strictly safer.

### Special notes for your reviewer

The `expandTemplate` function is unexported and has no callers outside this package, so the signature change is fully contained.

`jsonContentType` middleware was applied globally on the root router, forcing `Content-Type: application/json` on all responses including the embedded frontend's HTML/CSS/JS assets. Browsers refuse to execute JS served as `application/json`, breaking the production binary. Masked in dev because Vite serves the frontend on a separate port.

prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:

`jsonContentType` middleware was applied globally on the root router, forcing `Content-Type: application/json` on all responses including the embedded frontend's HTML/CSS/JS assets. Browsers refuse to execute JS served as `application/json`, breaking the production binary. Masked in dev because Vite serves the frontend on a separate port.

After this PR:

`jsonContentType` middleware is scoped to the `/api` route group only. Frontend assets are served with correct MIME types. Standalone JSON routes (`/health`) get correct content-type via `writeJSON()`.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Added `Content-Type` header setting directly in `writeJSON()` — this covers routes outside the `/api` group (e.g. `/health`) without needing to duplicate middleware or restructure the router. Redundant with the middleware for `/api` routes, but harmless and defensive.
- Moved `/api/version` from root router into the `/api` route group — it was registered via `r.Get("/api/version", ...)` on the root router, so it wouldn't receive the now-scoped middleware. Logically belongs in the group anyway.
- `/api/ws` (WebSocket) intentionally left on root router — it should **not** get `Content-Type: application/json`.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Removing the middleware entirely and relying solely on `writeJSON()` — viable but a larger behavioral change; keeping the middleware preserves defense-in-depth for any future `/api` handler that might not use `writeJSON`.

### Breaking changes

None. API responses are unchanged. Frontend assets now serve correctly.

### Special notes for your reviewer

`frontend/embed.go` had `w.Header().Del("Content-Type")` workarounds to undo the global middleware — those are removed since the root cause is fixed.

prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:
Single agent Docker image ships restic + rclone. Hooks needing database CLI tools (e.g. `sqlite3 .dump`) require users to build custom images.

After this PR:
Two agent image variants are published:

| Image | Tools | Use case |
|-------|-------|----------|
| `-agent` | restic + rclone | File/directory backups |
| `-agent-db` | restic + rclone + sqlite3 | Hooks that need database CLIs |

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

Restic + SQLite is a very common combination. Rather than requiring users to maintain custom Dockerfiles just to get `sqlite3`, we ship a curated variant.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- Separate Dockerfile (`Dockerfile.agent-db`) over a build-arg toggle — explicit, independently cacheable, no conditional logic in the build.
- Alpine `sqlite` package over a static binary download — simpler, gets security patches via `apk upgrade`, consistent with Alpine base.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Single image with all tools: bloats the slim image for users who don't need database tools.
- Multi-stage FROM the base agent image: complicates multi-arch builds and layer caching.

### Breaking changes

None. Existing `-agent` image is unchanged.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- `Dockerfile.agent-db` is identical to `Dockerfile.agent` except for one added `RUN apk add --no-cache sqlite` layer — easy to verify with `diff docker/Dockerfile.agent docker/Dockerfile.agent-db`.
- The `-agent-db` variant is designed to accumulate more database tools over time (pg_dump, mysqldump) as prerequisites for future built-in preset hook scripts (Option C from the issue).

prs.title: fix: exclude agent API key from REST API responses
prs.releaseNote: Security fix: agent API keys are no longer included in REST API responses for GET /agents and GET /agents/{id}.
prs.breakingChanges: Any client currently parsing `api_key` from agent REST responses will no longer receive it (which is the intended behavior — it should never have been exposed).
prs.body:
The `Agent` struct was serializing `APIKey` in every `GET /agents` and `GET /agents/{id}` response, leaking the gRPC authentication secret over the REST API.

### Change

**`server/internal/database/agents.go`**
- Tag `APIKey` with `json:"-"` instead of `json:"api_key,omitempty"` so the field is unconditionally excluded from JSON marshaling

```go
// Before
APIKey *string `json:"api_key,omitempty"`

// After
APIKey *string `json:"-"`
```

The frontend `Agent` interface never declared `api_key`, so no frontend changes are required. The field remains fully usable in Go (database reads/writes, gRPC approval flow) — only JSON serialization is suppressed.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The API key is a shared secret used for gRPC agent authentication. Exposing it over the REST API allows any caller with read access to impersonate agents.

The following tradeoffs were made:
- `json:"-"` on the struct field is the minimal, zero-abstraction fix. A separate response DTO would work but adds indirection with no benefit here since the frontend never consumed this field.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Response DTO that omits the field — rejected as unnecessary complexity given the frontend already ignores the field.

### Breaking changes

Any client currently parsing `api_key` from agent REST responses will no longer receive it (which is the intended behavior — it should never have been exposed).

### Special notes for your reviewer

Verify no internal server-side code relies on the JSON representation of `Agent.APIKey` (e.g., event serialization, audit logging).

prs.title: feat: migrate server logging to log/slog and fix silent error discards
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR:

All server logging used `log.Printf` with no severity levels, no structured fields, and several code paths silently discarded errors (e.g., `pushConfigForPlan` returned without logging on DB failures).

After this PR:

All 15 server source files use `log/slog` with appropriate severity levels and structured key-value fields. Silent error discards are fixed.
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:

All server logging used `log.Printf` with no severity levels, no structured fields, and several code paths silently discarded errors (e.g., `pushConfigForPlan` returned without logging on DB failures).

After this PR:

All 15 server source files use `log/slog` with appropriate severity levels and structured key-value fields. Silent error discards are fixed.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

Unstructured `log.Printf` output cannot be filtered, aggregated, or alerted on in production. `log/slog` is stdlib (Go 1.21+), zero new dependencies, and the codebase already uses it on the agent side.

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Used `slog.TextHandler` (not JSON) as default — keeps dev-friendly output; can be swapped to `slog.JSONHandler` for production via a config flag later.
- `os.Exit(1)` in server startup goroutines preserves original `log.Fatalf` behavior — a pre-existing pattern, not changed here to keep scope tight.
- Audit logging deferred to a future issue per maintainer request.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Third-party loggers (zerolog, zap) — unnecessary given slog is now stdlib and sufficient.

### Breaking changes

None. Log output format changes from unstructured to structured text, but no API or behavioral changes.

### Special notes for your reviewer

**Structured logging migration** — mechanical replacement across all server packages:

- `log.Printf("...", args)` → `slog.Info/Warn/Error("msg", "key", val, ...)`
- `log.Fatalf` → `slog.Error` + `os.Exit(1)` (slog has no Fatal level)
- Severity levels assigned by intent: `Info` for normal ops, `Warn` for recoverable issues, `Error` for failures

**Silent error fixes:**

- `pushConfigForPlan` (hooks.go) — previously `if err != nil || plan == nil { return }` silently swallowed DB errors. Now logs with `slog.Error`.
- `reorderHooksHandler` (hooks.go) — `ListHooks` error was discarded via `_`. Now captured and logged.

Before:
```go
plan, err := db.GetPlan(ctx, planID)
if err != nil || plan == nil {
    return // silent discard
}
```

After:
```go
plan, err := db.GetPlan(ctx, planID)
if err != nil {
    slog.Error("failed to get plan for config push", "plan_id", planID, "error", err)
    return
}
if plan == nil {
    return
}
```

prs.title: Enforce per-plan concurrency: abort duplicate triggers, allow cross-plan parallelism
prs.releaseNote: Agent now enforces a per-plan concurrency policy: different backup plans may run in parallel, but a trigger (manual or scheduled) for a plan that is already running is rejected and recorded as a job with status "aborted" so it shows up in job history.
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR:
The scheduler tracked a single `currentJob` and `TriggerNow` launched a goroutine unconditionally. A manual trigger overlapping a scheduled run (or rapid re-clicks) silently overwrote the first job's status. There was no policy — concurrent execution was an accident of implementation.

After this PR:
Concurrency policy is explicit and enforced in the agent:
- **Different plans** may run in parallel (tracked in a per-plan map).
- **Same plan** cannot. A second trigger is rejected immediately and recorded as a `JobReport{status: "aborted", reason: "plan already running"}` so operators see it in job history.

Changes:
- `agent/internal/scheduler/scheduler.go` — replace `currentJob *JobStatus` with `currentJobs map[string]*JobStatus` (key = plan ID). New `runJob` + `tryStartJob` helpers; both `TriggerNow` and the cron closure funnel through `runJob`. - Tests — scheduler tests cover same-plan rejection, cross-plan parallelism, earliest-plan heartbeat selection, and the aborted-report emission.
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:
The scheduler tracked a single `currentJob` and `TriggerNow` launched a goroutine unconditionally. A manual trigger overlapping a scheduled run (or rapid re-clicks) silently overwrote the first job's status. There was no policy — concurrent execution was an accident of implementation.

After this PR:
Concurrency policy is explicit and enforced in the agent:
- **Different plans** may run in parallel (tracked in a per-plan map).
- **Same plan** cannot. A second trigger is rejected immediately and recorded as a `JobReport{status: "aborted", reason: "plan already running"}` so operators see it in job history.

Changes:
- `agent/internal/scheduler/scheduler.go` — replace `currentJob *JobStatus` with `currentJobs map[string]*JobStatus` (key = plan ID). New `runJob` + `tryStartJob` helpers; both `TriggerNow` and the cron closure funnel through `runJob`. On conflict, a synthesized aborted `JobReport` is pushed through the reporter. `JobStatusFunc` returns the earliest-started running job, keeping the existing single-job `RunningJob` heartbeat proto compatible.
- `server/internal/grpcserver/report.go` — `storeJobReport` special-cases `status == "aborted"`: always create a new row, never overwrite an actively running job via `FindPlannedJob`.
- Frontend — `Job.status` / `HeatmapRun.status` unions, `StatusBadge`, `RunHeatmap.cellColor`, and the `JobsView` filter learn `aborted` (neutral gray, so red stays reserved for real failures).
- `docs/agent-further-considerations.md` §5 — documents the resolved policy and restic's repository locking (see below).
- Tests — scheduler tests cover same-plan rejection, cross-plan parallelism, earliest-plan heartbeat selection, and the aborted-report emission.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:
- **Reject, don't queue.** A depth-1 queue was considered and rejected (per the issue): a pending job that never runs is confusing to operators; fail-fast with a visible `aborted` entry is clearer.
- **No proto change.** The issue suggested making `RunningJob` repeated. Instead, the per-plan map is agent-internal and heartbeats surface the earliest running plan. The authoritative per-run record is the `JobReport` at completion, so UI fidelity is unaffected in the common single-plan case and no breaking proto migration is needed.
- **No agent-level repository lock.** Restic already serializes repository access with file-based locks: `backup` takes a shared lock (concurrent backups — including across machines — are safe); `forget`/`prune`/`check` take an exclusive lock. If restic's lock is contended, the error surfaces as a normal backup failure and the user adjusts their schedule. Adding a second locking layer would only duplicate what restic already guarantees.
- **Aborted reports bypass `FindPlannedJob`.** Otherwise an `aborted` report would overwrite the row of the job it was rejected *by*.

The following alternatives were considered:
- Per-repository locking at the agent — rejected; restic handles it.
- Queueing overlapping triggers — rejected; hidden waiting is worse than a visible rejection.
- Changing `RunningJob` to `repeated` — deferred; not required to meet the policy and would force a proto rev.

Links to places where the discussion took place: issue comment from @tryy3 on restic locking is addressed in `docs/agent-further-considerations.md` §5.

### Breaking changes

None. Proto is unchanged. DB `jobs.status` has no CHECK constraint, so the new `aborted` value requires no migration.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- `JobStatusFunc` intentionally still returns a single `*JobStatus` (earliest-started) to avoid a proto change. If/when the UI needs to display all running plans simultaneously, promote `RunningJob` to `repeated` in a follow-up.
- The aborted carve-out in `storeJobReport` is the one spot where server behaviour is status-sensitive — worth a careful read.

Approvers are expected to review this list.

Agent now enforces a per-plan concurrency policy: different backup plans may run in parallel, but a trigger (manual or scheduled) for a plan that is already running is rejected and recorded as a job with status "aborted" so it shows up in job history.

prs.title: agent: stream restic output and bound stdout/stderr capture
prs.releaseNote: agent: cap memory used to capture restic subprocess output. `restic backup --json` is now consumed line-by-line so per-file status messages are discarded instead of buffered, and captured stderr (including the field stored on backup reports) is truncated to the last 4 KiB. Fixes runaway agent RSS growth on long-running or large backups.
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR:

`runRestic` in `agent/internal/executor/restic.go` buffered the entire restic stdout/stderr into `bytes.Buffer`s before returning. For `restic backup --json` against a large repository (one JSON message per file, plus a `status` update every ~100 ms), the stdout buffer grew to multi-GB and was the prime suspect for the agent reaching ~13 GB RSS during long-running backups. The full stderr was also propagated unchanged into wrapped errors and into a single structured-log attribute persisted with the report.

After this PR:

Agent memory during a backup is independent of the number of files restic processes. Per-file `status` messages are parsed and discarded immediately; only the parsed `summary` struct and a small bounded diagnostic tail are retained. Stderr is capped to the last 4 KiB everywhere it is captured.

Changes:

- **`tailBuffer`** — thread-safe `io.Writer` retaining only the last N bytes, with a `...[truncated]...` marker on overflow.
- **`streamRestic`** — drains stdout via `cmd.StdoutPipe()` + `bufio.Scanner` (1 MiB max line) into a per-line callback, captures stderr directly into a 4 KiB `tailBuffer`, then `cmd.Wait()`s.
- **`runRestic`** — now wraps `streamRestic`, accumulating stdout into a 1 MiB tail buffer. Existing `(stdout, stderr, err)` contract preserved for `Snapshots`, `ListFiles`, `Forget`, `Prune`, `Restore`, `EnsureRepo` — only the cap is new.
- **`Backup`** — consumes JSON output incrementally via `streamRestic`: discards `status` messages, retains the `summary` struct, keeps a 200-line ring of non-status lines for use in the "no summary" error path. Wrapped-error stderr is now bounded.
- **`BackupResult.Stderr`** — now the bounded 4 KiB tail, transitively bounding the log attribute and persisted report field.
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:

`runRestic` in `agent/internal/executor/restic.go` buffered the entire restic stdout/stderr into `bytes.Buffer`s before returning. For `restic backup --json` against a large repository (one JSON message per file, plus a `status` update every ~100 ms), the stdout buffer grew to multi-GB and was the prime suspect for the agent reaching ~13 GB RSS during long-running backups. The full stderr was also propagated unchanged into wrapped errors and into a single structured-log attribute persisted with the report.

After this PR:

Agent memory during a backup is independent of the number of files restic processes. Per-file `status` messages are parsed and discarded immediately; only the parsed `summary` struct and a small bounded diagnostic tail are retained. Stderr is capped to the last 4 KiB everywhere it is captured.

Changes:

- **`tailBuffer`** — thread-safe `io.Writer` retaining only the last N bytes, with a `...[truncated]...` marker on overflow.
- **`streamRestic`** — drains stdout via `cmd.StdoutPipe()` + `bufio.Scanner` (1 MiB max line) into a per-line callback, captures stderr directly into a 4 KiB `tailBuffer`, then `cmd.Wait()`s.
- **`runRestic`** — now wraps `streamRestic`, accumulating stdout into a 1 MiB tail buffer. Existing `(stdout, stderr, err)` contract preserved for `Snapshots`, `ListFiles`, `Forget`, `Prune`, `Restore`, `EnsureRepo` — only the cap is new.
- **`Backup`** — consumes JSON output incrementally via `streamRestic`: discards `status` messages, retains the `summary` struct, keeps a 200-line ring of non-status lines for use in the "no summary" error path. Wrapped-error stderr is now bounded.
- **`BackupResult.Stderr`** — now the bounded 4 KiB tail, transitively bounding the log attribute and persisted report field.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The fix is scoped to `restic.go` and keeps `runRestic`'s signature so all other subprocess wrappers are untouched. `Backup` is the only caller that needed to switch to the streaming variant because it is the only one whose output is unbounded by design.

The following tradeoffs were made:

- `runRestic` retains the **last** N bytes on overflow, so a truncated `Snapshots`/`ListFiles` response will fail JSON-parsing loudly rather than silently corrupt — preferred over OOM. In practice these outputs sit well under 1 MiB.
- The 200-line backup tail and the truncation marker are kept simple rather than introducing a structured ring-buffer type.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Replacing every `runRestic` caller with a streaming API — larger blast radius for little gain since only `Backup` produces unbounded output.
- `runtime/debug.SetMemoryLimit` as the sole fix — defense-in-depth only; does not prevent GC thrashing under sustained allocation pressure.

Links to places where the discussion took place: issue thread.

### Breaking changes

None. Public types and method signatures are unchanged. `BackupResult.Stderr` is now bounded to ~4 KiB (preceded by a truncation marker if it overflowed); downstream consumers treat it as opaque text.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- Tests use a shell-script fake `restic` placed on `PATH` via `t.Setenv` (skipped on Windows).
- The truncation marker (`...[truncated]...\n`) is intentionally human-readable and appears at the **start** of the captured tail.
- `bufio.Scanner` max line is 1 MiB — needed because `backup --json` `status` messages embed `current_files` and can exceed the 64 KiB default.

prs.title: fix: use per-attempt context for gRPC stream so recv goroutine unblocks on disconnect
prs.releaseNote: Fixed gRPC stream reconnect stalling for minutes on half-open TCP connections. The agent now unblocks immediately on disconnect and includes client-side keepalive for faster dead connection detection.
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR:

`Run()` opens the gRPC stream with the caller's `ctx` but coordinates goroutine shutdown via a derived `runCtx`. Cancelling `runCtx` does not unblock `stream.Recv()` because the stream is bound to the outer context. On half-open TCP (NAT timeout, network blip, ungraceful server kill), the recv goroutine blocks in `Recv()` until TCP keepalive fires — potentially minutes — stalling reconnect.

After this PR:

The stream is opened with a per-attempt `streamCtx` derived from `ctx`. When `Run` exits, `streamCancel()` immediately unblocks `stream.Recv()` with `context.Canceled`. Additionally, gRPC client keepalive pings (30s interval, 10s timeout) detect half-open TCP within ~40s without relying on OS defaults.
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:

`Run()` opens the gRPC stream with the caller's `ctx` but coordinates goroutine shutdown via a derived `runCtx`. Cancelling `runCtx` does not unblock `stream.Recv()` because the stream is bound to the outer context. On half-open TCP (NAT timeout, network blip, ungraceful server kill), the recv goroutine blocks in `Recv()` until TCP keepalive fires — potentially minutes — stalling reconnect.

After this PR:

The stream is opened with a per-attempt `streamCtx` derived from `ctx`. When `Run` exits, `streamCancel()` immediately unblocks `stream.Recv()` with `context.Canceled`. Additionally, gRPC client keepalive pings (30s interval, 10s timeout) detect half-open TCP within ~40s without relying on OS defaults.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The fix is the minimal correct change: move `context.WithCancel` above `Connect()` so the same context governs both the stream and goroutine coordination.

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Keepalive `Time: 30s` matches the default heartbeat interval. Aggressive enough for prompt detection, conservative enough to avoid unnecessary traffic.
- `PermitWithoutStream: true` keeps probing even when idle, which matters for long-idle streams between heartbeats.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Adding a `select { case <-runCtx.Done() }` in the recv goroutine — insufficient, `Recv()` still blocks.
- Shorter keepalive intervals — unnecessary given the context-cancel fix handles the primary case.

### Breaking changes

None. The stream context is still derived from the caller's `ctx`, so external cancellation semantics are unchanged.

### Special notes for your reviewer

Key diff in `stream.go`:
```go
// Before: stream bound to outer ctx, runCtx only coordinates goroutines
stream, err := s.client.client.Connect(ctx)
runCtx, runCancel := context.WithCancel(ctx)

// After: single context governs both stream and goroutine lifecycle
streamCtx, streamCancel := context.WithCancel(ctx)
stream, err := s.client.client.Connect(streamCtx)
```

New bufconn-based tests assert `Run` returns within 500ms of cancel (not minutes).

prs.title: fix: serialize gRPC stream sends through dedicated send goroutine
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR:

`stream.Send` was called concurrently from the send goroutine (heartbeats, live logs) and the recv goroutine (`handleConfig` → config ack, `handleCommand` → command result). This violates the gRPC streaming contract and is a data race.

After this PR:

All `stream.Send` calls are serialized through a single send goroutine via a buffered outbound channel. The recv goroutine never touches the stream's send path. This is combined with main's `streamCtx/streamCancel` pattern (from the recv-unblock fix) so that context cancellation properly unblocks both goroutines.
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR:

`stream.Send` was called concurrently from the send goroutine (heartbeats, live logs) and the recv goroutine (`handleConfig` → config ack, `handleCommand` → command result). This violates the gRPC streaming contract and is a data race.

After this PR:

All `stream.Send` calls are serialized through a single send goroutine via a buffered outbound channel. The recv goroutine never touches the stream's send path. This is combined with main's `streamCtx/streamCancel` pattern (from the recv-unblock fix) so that context cancellation properly unblocks both goroutines.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The gRPC-Go docs are explicit: *"It is not safe to call `SendMsg` on the same stream in different goroutines."* The race is latent — it manifests when a config push or command arrives during a heartbeat/log-flush window.

The following tradeoffs were made:

- `handleConfig`/`handleCommand` are dispatched in separate goroutines from the recv loop. This keeps the recv loop non-blocking (per maintainer guidance) at the cost of slightly more goroutine churn. The `handlerWg` ensures graceful drain on shutdown.
- Channel-based serialization over `sync.Mutex` — cleaner fit with the existing select loop and lets the send goroutine apply uniform error handling.

The following alternatives were considered:

- **Mutex wrapping every `stream.Send`**: Works but scatters lock acquisition across goroutines; harder to reason about shutdown ordering.
- **Synchronous handlers in recv goroutine**: Simpler but blocks message reception during slow command execution.

### Breaking changes

None. Internal refactor only; no API or proto changes.

### Special notes for your reviewer

Key changes in `agent/internal/grpcclient/stream.go`:

- **`outboundCh`** (`chan *backupv1.AgentMessage`, buffer 32): funnels config acks and command results into the send goroutine
- **Send goroutine** gains a `case msg, ok := <-outboundCh` arm in its select, and uses `streamCtx.Done()` (from main's recv-unblock fix) instead of a separate `runCtx`
- **`handleConfig` / `handleCommand`** signature changes from `stream` param to `outboundCh chan<-` param — they enqueue instead of sending
- **`handlerWg`** tracks in-flight handler goroutines; shutdown sequence: `streamCancel()` → `handlerWg.Wait()` → `close(outboundCh)` → send goroutine drains remaining messages → `CloseSend()`

Tests include both mock-based send-serialisation tests (tracking concurrent `Send` calls via atomic counter) and bufconn-based integration tests (from main's recv-unblock fix verifying context cancellation and server disconnect behavior).

prs.title: agent: dispatch stream commands concurrently with configurable per-kind timeouts
prs.releaseNote: Agent: gRPC commands now run concurrently with per-kind timeouts (defaults: 24h for backup/restore, 5m for list/browse snapshots, 30s for filesystem browse), so a slow or hung restic/rclone invocation no longer blocks heartbeats, config pushes, or other commands on the same connection. The timeouts are tunable from the Settings page (global defaults) and from each agent's detail page (per-agent overrides).
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR: the recv goroutine in `agent/internal/grpcclient/stream.go` invoked `handleCommand` synchronously, so a single slow command (hung rclone backend, long restic restore) blocked all further `ServerMessage`s — heartbeats, config pushes, and new commands — for the lifetime of that call. There was also no per-command deadline; only the process-wide stream context bounded execution.

After this PR:

- `handleCommand` spawns a goroutine per command and returns immediately; the recv loop keeps draining the stream.
- Each command runs under `context.WithTimeout(streamCtx, sh.commandTimeout(cmd))` with kind-specific defaults (now overridable from the server, see below):
  - `TriggerBackup` / `TriggerRestore`: 24h
  - `ListSnapshots` / `BrowseSnapshot`: 5m
  - `BrowseFilesystem`: 30s
  - default: 5m
- In-flight handler goroutines are tracked by a `sync.WaitGroup` (`handlerWg`) and cancelled via the stream context on shutdown; `Run` waits for them before returning.
- All outbound writes are funneled through the existing `outboundCh` channel into the single send goroutine, so `stream.Send` is never called concurrently. Per-command results, config acks, and live logs all share that channel.
- `onCommand` signature gained a `context.Context` so handlers receive the per-command ctx; `exec.CommandContext` in the restic executor already honors it, so a timed-out backend is killed cleanly.
- Per-command timeouts are now **configurable from the frontend** at two levels:
  - **Global defaults** — six new settings keys (`command_timeout_backup_seconds`, `…_restore_seconds`, `…_list_snapshots_seconds`, `…_browse_snapshot_seconds`, `…_browse_filesystem_seconds`, `…_default_seconds`) editable from the Settings page under a new "Agent Command Timeouts" section.
  - **Per-agent overrides** — stored in a new `command_timeouts` JSON column on `agents` (added via an idempotent `ALTER TABLE` migration helper) and editable from a collapsible "Command Timeouts Override" panel on the agent detail page, with a "custom" badge and a "Reset to Global" button.
- A new `CommandTimeouts` proto message is added to `AgentConfig` (field 8). The `configpush` resolver merges global settings with the per-agent override and ships the result; the agent stores them on `StreamHandler` and `commandTimeout(cmd)` honors them, falling back to the compiled-in defaults for any field left at 0. A new `PUT /api/agents/{id}/command-timeouts` endpoint persists the per-agent override and triggers an immediate config push.

- Per-command timeouts are now **configurable from the frontend** at two levels:
  - **Global defaults** — six new settings keys (`command_timeout_backup_seconds`, `…_restore_seconds`, `…_list_snapshots_seconds`, `…_browse_snapshot_seconds`, `…_browse_filesystem_seconds`, `…_default_seconds`) editable from the Settings page under a new "Agent Command Timeouts" section.
  - **Per-agent overrides** — stored in a new `command_timeouts` JSON column on `agents` (added via an idempotent `ALTER TABLE` migration helper) and editable from a collapsible "Command Timeouts Override" panel on the agent detail page, with a "custom" badge and a "Reset to Global" button.
- A new `CommandTimeouts` proto message is added to `AgentConfig` (field 8). The `configpush` resolver merges global settings with the per-agent override and ships the result; the agent stores them on `StreamHandler` and `commandTimeout(cmd)` honors them, falling back to the compiled-in defaults for any field left at 0. A new `PUT /api/agents/{id}/command-timeouts` endpoint persists the per-agent override and triggers an immediate config push.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- **Fixed per-kind timeouts** rather than "timeout since last log line". Restic's output is currently buffered (`cmd.Run()` with `bytes.Buffer` stdout/stderr in `runRestic`), so an idle-watchdog would need streaming stdout first. Per the issue's agent note, falling back to generous per-kind ceilings (now tunable globally and per-agent from the UI) is acceptable until log streaming lands.
- **Unbounded goroutines per command** rather than a worker pool. Command fan-in is driven by the server, which already serializes reasonable volumes; a pool adds queuing semantics that would need their own rejection/telemetry story. Revisit if this becomes a footgun.
- **Stream-scoped cancellation** (derived from the stream context): in-flight commands die on reconnect, which is correct since their results would be undeliverable anyway.
- **JSON column for per-agent overrides** rather than a separate normalized table. The shape is small and tightly coupled to the proto message, so a single nullable `command_timeouts TEXT` column avoids a join and migrates trivially.
- **Merge-on-resolve strategy**: the resolver layers per-agent values over global values per-field, with 0 meaning "inherit". This keeps the data model sparse — you only persist what you explicitly override.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Running commands on the existing send goroutine — rejected, same head-of-line blocking.
- A dedicated `sendMu` mutex around `stream.Send` — used in an earlier revision but dropped after the merge with `main`, which had migrated `stream.go` to a channel-based send-serialization design (`outboundCh` + dedicated send goroutine). Per-command goroutines now enqueue results onto that channel instead of holding a mutex.
- Per-command cancellation on duplicate-target commands — not implemented; the server does not currently send duplicates and the issue marks it optional.
- Hardcoded timeouts only — rejected based on review feedback; values that benefit from tuning over time should be configurable at runtime.

Links to places where the discussion took place: linked issue, PR review comment.

### Breaking changes

None at the wire level — the new `AgentConfig.command_timeouts` proto field is additive and unset means "use agent defaults". Internal API: `grpcclient.NewStreamHandler`'s `onCommand` callback now takes `(ctx context.Context, cmd *backupv1.Command)`, and `handleCommand` takes `(ctx, outboundCh, cmd)`. The only caller (`agent/cmd/agent/main.go`) is updated in this PR.

Schema: an idempotent migration adds the `command_timeouts TEXT` column to `agents`; existing rows are unaffected (column defaults to `NULL`, meaning "no override").

### Special notes for your reviewer

- `commandTimeout` is now a method on `StreamHandler` (not a package-level function) so it can read the configured overrides under `cmdTimeoutsMu`.
- Defaults still live as `default*CommandTimeout` constants and are the single knob for tuning the built-in fallbacks; the UI exposes the global-setting overrides on top of those.
- Per-command goroutines enqueue their `CommandResult` on `outboundCh` with a `select`/`streamCtx.Done()` guard, so a stream shutdown during a long-running command does not block the handler.
- `addColumnIfMissing` in `server/internal/database/migrations.go` is a small helper for additive column migrations on SQLite (which has no `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`); reusable for future columns.
- Unit tests cover `commandTimeout` kind selection, the invariant that backup/restore budgets exceed browse budgets, and that server-pushed `CommandTimeouts` overrides take effect via `applyCommandTimeouts`. The bufconn-based recv-loop tests from `main` are kept and updated for the new `onCommand(ctx, cmd)` and `handleCommand(ctx, outboundCh, cmd)` signatures.
- This PR has been merged with `main` multiple times as new fixes (hook subprocess env-leak, identity APIKey data-race, etc.) landed there. The latest merge takes main's version of unrelated files (`.gitignore`, `restic.go`, `identity.go`, `scheduler.go`, `restic_test.go`) verbatim, and re-applies the per-command timeout pieces on top of main's current `stream.go`/`stream_test.go` so that main's `identityMu` removal and `GetAPIKey()`/`SetAPIKey()` race-fix are preserved alongside the timeout feature.
- The latest merge with `main` is finalized as a real two-parent merge commit (parent 1: previous PR tip, parent 2: current `origin/main`), so `git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main HEAD` now passes and the GitHub PR page no longer reports topological merge conflicts. Earlier merges had been getting flattened to single-parent commits on push, which is what kept tripping the conflict indicator even though the file content was already correct.
- Re-ran `gofmt -w` on `server/internal/api/agents.go` after the latest merge — the new `*configpush.CommandTimeouts` field on `agentResponse` widened the longest struct-tag column, so the surrounding tags needed re-aligning to satisfy the CI fmt check.

prs.title: fix: scheduler always interprets cron expressions in UTC
prs.releaseNote: Cron schedules are now always evaluated in UTC. Agents that were running in a non-UTC local timezone will see scheduled jobs shift to their UTC-equivalent time. This eliminates timezone drift across agents and DST-related skipped/duplicated runs.
prs.breakingChanges: Agents previously running in a non-UTC local timezone will see scheduled jobs shift to their UTC equivalent time. This is the intended, correct behavior.
prs.whatThisPrDoes:
Before this PR: `cron.New()` defaults to `time.Local`, causing the same cron expression to fire at different absolute times on agents in different timezones, and to skip or duplicate runs across DST transitions.

After this PR: The cron scheduler always interprets expressions in UTC via `cron.WithLocation(time.UTC)`, regardless of the agent host's `TZ` environment variable or `/etc/localtime`.
prs.body:
### What this PR does

Before this PR: `cron.New()` defaults to `time.Local`, causing the same cron expression to fire at different absolute times on agents in different timezones, and to skip or duplicate runs across DST transitions.

After this PR: The cron scheduler always interprets expressions in UTC via `cron.WithLocation(time.UTC)`, regardless of the agent host's `TZ` environment variable or `/etc/localtime`.

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

Cron expressions pushed from the server have no embedded timezone; the only sensible single-source-of-truth is UTC. `cron.WithLocation` is the idiomatic `robfig/cron/v3` mechanism for pinning the interpreter timezone — one-line fix, zero API change.

The following tradeoffs were made:

Per-plan timezone support (carrying a `timezone` field in the proto) was left out of scope. UTC-by-default is the safe, deterministic baseline; per-plan overrides can be layered on top later.

The following alternatives were considered:

Adding a `timezone` field to the `BackupPlan` proto for per-plan overrides. Deferred — adds proto churn and frontend work without being necessary to fix the immediate DST/drift bug.

### Breaking changes

Agents previously running in a non-UTC local timezone will see scheduled jobs shift to their UTC equivalent time. This is the intended, correct behavior.

### Special notes for your reviewer

No proto changes. No API changes. Only the cron constructor call site is touched.

The branch has been rebased/merged onto `main` (commit e83f2d8), which introduced a concurrent per-plan job guard (`currentJobs` map, `tryStartJob`, `runJob`). The merge conflict was in the `New` function; the resolution keeps both `cron.WithLocation(time.UTC)` from this PR and the `currentJobs` initialisation from `main`.
